author: Varshank Shukla
headline: Data & Business Analyst | Product Analytics | Funnel Analysis | SQL | Python | Power BI | Tableau | IIIT Bangalore
text:
“SQL is easy.”
Said every Data Analyst… who has never worked with real data.
Me: You know SQL?
Candidate: Yes, very comfortable.
Cool.
Then I ask:
You have a table of user events (clicks, page views, sessions).
👉 Write a query to find “engaged users”
Confidence drops instantly.
Because suddenly:
What counts as engagement?
Is a page refresh a real interaction?
Do we filter bots?
Do background events count?
And the best part?
Everyone starts writing queries…
👉 Without defining the metric first.
Here’s the uncomfortable truth:
Most analysts don’t struggle with SQL.
👉 They struggle with defining what they’re measuring.
SQL doesn’t make you an analyst.
👉 It just makes you fast at counting things you don’t understand.
And if your metric definition is wrong…
Congratulations!
You just built a dashboard no one should trust.

text:
SQL Interview Questions You Can’t Ignore if You’re Targeting Walmart, Google, Amazon & Top PBCs (𝟮𝟮.𝟳–𝟰𝟮 𝗟𝗣𝗔)

Most professionals think SQL is “easy”…
But in reality, SQL is what decides who clears the final technical round.

Here are real-world SQL problems that frequently come up in interviews 👇

1️⃣ Top-selling product per category
→ Use window functions
→ Follow-ups: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK, tie handling

2️⃣ Deduplicate records (keep latest)
→ Focus on deterministic logic
→ Window functions, ordering, QUALIFY

3️⃣ Rolling averages (7-day / 30-day)
→ PARTITION + window frames
→ Performance at scale

4️⃣ Orders on 3 consecutive days
→ LAG + date logic + grouping

5️⃣ % contribution to total revenue (no subqueries)
→ Window aggregates mastery

6️⃣ Slow group-by due to data skew
→ Indexing, stats, distribution keys
→ Query optimization thinking

7️⃣ Pivot monthly revenue dynamically
→ Static vs dynamic pivots
→ Performance trade-offs

8️⃣ First-time purchasers in a month
→ MIN(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user)

9️⃣ Sessionization (30-min inactivity)
→ LAG + timestamp handling
→ Common in Walmart / Google interviews

🔟 Debug a slow query (3× slower)
→ Query plan analysis
→ Join strategy, stats, cardinality
→ Predicate pushdown, materialization

These are actual SQL challenges asked in PBC interviews. And this is where most people struggle. They prepare basic SQL, but interviews test real-world data thinking.

text:
📊 SQL Interview Challenge – Mutual Friends

Here’s an interesting SQL problem that tests your understanding of joins, subqueries, and set logic:

🧾 Table Structure
CREATE TABLE microsoft_users([user_id] INT, [user_name] varchar(30));

CREATE TABLE microsoft_friends([user_id] INT, friend_id INT);

 📥 Sample Data
INSERT INTO microsoft_users VALUES (1, 'Karl'), (2, 'Hans'), (3, 'Emma'), (4,'Emma'), (5, 'Mike'), (6, 'Lucas'), (7, 'Sarah'), (8, 'Lucas'), (9, 'Anna'), (10,'John');

INSERT INTO microsoft_friends VALUES (1,3),(1,5),(2,3),(2,4),(3,1),(3,2),(3,6),(4,7),(5,8),(6,9),(7,10),(8,6),(9,10),(10,7),(10,9);

🎯 Task
 Find the mutual friends between Karl and Hans
👉 Conditions:
• There is only one user named Karl and one named Hans
• Return users who are friends with both Karl and Hans

📌 Expected Output
 • user_id
 • user_name
 • Results should show only mutual friends
